name: Identifiable victim effect
statement: People are said to give more to one named and pictured victim than to statistics about many, but the bias-corrected pooled estimate is near zero and preregistered replications have not found it.
meaning: The claim compares two ways of describing the same need. One names a person, gives an age, and shows a photograph. The other gives a number. Helping is held to be higher in the first case, which would mean charity tracks how a cause is presented rather than how much good the money does. Three mechanisms are usually offered. Proportion dominance says an identified victim is her own reference group, so helping her rescues 100% of those at risk. The affect heuristic says a specific face produces sympathy and a number does not. Perceived impact says people give when they can picture what the money changes. The three make different predictions, and the literature has not settled which of them, if any, is carrying the effect.

origin.who: Karen E. Jenni and George Loewenstein
origin.note: Their paper is titled "Explaining the 'Identifiable Victim Effect'" and opens with an epigraph from Thomas Schelling's 1968 discussion of the individual and the statistical life. They write that they have seen no explicit treatment of the effect in the helping literature or the empathy literature. Jenni and Loewenstein took the effect as given and tested four candidate causes; the effect itself was not what they set out to demonstrate.

evidence: Jenni and Loewenstein ran two hypothetical scenario studies. The first went to 70 undergraduates at Carnegie Mellon, 30 visitors to a mall south of Boston and 27 visitors to two student centres. The second went to 121 adult visitors to Pittsburgh International Airport. Nothing was donated. Respondents rated how important an intervention was, or how responsible they would feel. Only one of the four candidate causes came through. People gave higher priority to a safety programme saving 25 of 25 people at risk than to one saving 25 of 50,000, which is proportion of the reference group. Vividness did nothing. In the second study a victim trapped after an earthquake was described generically, described in detail, or described with a picture. Respondents said they cared least when the picture was included, F(2, 111) not significant. Small, Loewenstein and Slovic put real money on the table ten years later. Participants at a university in Pennsylvania completed an unrelated survey, were paid five one-dollar bills, and could seal any of it into an envelope for Save the Children. The money went to the charity. Study 1, on 121 people, found an identifiable victim raised donations to $2.12 against $1.21 for statistics, F(1, 115) = 6.75, p < .05, partial eta squared .06. Study 3, on 159 people, produced the pair everyone quotes, and it is printed only in a bar chart: $2.38 for Rokia, a seven-year-old girl from Mali shown with a photograph, against $1.14 for four sentences of famine statistics about Malawi, Zambia, Angola and Ethiopia. The text reports the test as F(2) = 5.67, p < .01, partial eta squared .07, with no second degrees-of-freedom figure. Presenting Rokia together with the statistics dropped giving to $1.43, and the paper's argument is about that drop rather than about the gap. Kogut and Ritov added the singularity claim, that the effect holds for one victim and not for a group. Their Study 2 in the Journal of Behavioral Decision Making ran 112 Hebrew University undergraduates in a two-by-two design, and identification interacted with singularity, F(1, 108) = 7.12, p < 0.009. Majumder and colleagues recompute that interaction as partial eta squared .062, 90% CI .01 to .15. The name singularity effect comes from the title of Kogut and Ritov's second 2005 paper, in Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, which used real money. Its Experiment 1 paid 153 Hebrew University students 20 shekels each and let them give any of it away. The interaction again held, F(1, 149) = 13.036, p < .001, with the identified single child drawing a mean of 10.71 shekels against 5.03 for the identified group of eight. Majumder's group define the singularity effect as the tendency to give more aid to a single victim than to a group of victims facing the same need.

replication.headline: Three preregistered tests of the seminal paradigms found nothing, and a bias-corrected reanalysis of the only meta-analysis puts the pooled effect at r = 0.002.
replication.detail: Maier, Wong and Feldman reanalysed the 41 effects collected by Lee and Feeley with robust Bayesian meta-analysis. They describe the published pooled estimate as r = .05, obtained after a visual inspection of funnel plots, and reach the opposite reading: moderate evidence for publication bias, BF01 = 0.11, strong evidence for the absence of an average effect, BF01 = 14.93, and a model-averaged estimate of r = 0.002, 95% CI 0 to 0.004. They note that one study in the dataset, with 12,802 participants, returns r = 0.004. Their own test, which they call a far replication rather than a close one, merged Small, Loewenstein and Slovic's Studies 1 and 3 into a single design and ran it on 1,004 MTurk participants with hypothetical donations. They found no identifiable victim effect, partial eta squared .000, 95% CI .000 to .003, and no debiasing effect, .001, 95% CI .000 to .012. Identifiable against statistical came out at t(998) = 0.097, p = 1.00, d = 0.01, 95% CI -0.16 to 0.14, with a Bayes factor of 11.57 favouring the null. The one result they did find across all three identifiability conditions, F(2, 998) = 3.91, p = .02, partial eta squared .008, came from lower giving in the joint condition, and they caution against over-interpreting it. Majumder, Tai, Ziano and Feldman preregistered a close replication of Kogut and Ritov's Study 2 on 1,835 participants after exclusions, and found the singularity by identifiability interaction at partial eta squared .00, 90% CI 0.00 to 0.00. Mayiwar and seven colleagues added a third preregistered null while targeting compassion fade, entry 232. Their extension put a picture-free, name-free statistical condition, n = 174, alongside the identified conditions of the same Save the Children paradigm, on 1,207 US participants, and found no difference between any of them on donations, need, affect or perceived impact, partial eta squared at most .011. That work is a preprint posted on PsyArXiv in August 2026 and not a published article. Outside the laboratory, Lesner and Rasmussen mailed 25,797 prior donors of a Danish charity either an identifiable or a statistical appeal and report that the identifiable letter "did not result in significantly larger donations". Moche, Karlsson and Västfjäll ran five studies on 7,996 people and found no identifiability effect on donations in three of them; in a fourth the unidentified condition gave more, F(1, 1624) = 16.27, p < .001, partial eta squared .010.

study.cite: Maier, M., Wong, Y. C., & Feldman, G. (2024). Revisiting and rethinking the identifiable victim effect: Replication and extension of Small, Loewenstein, and Slovic (2007). Collabra: Psychology, 9(1), 90203.

limits: No well-powered replication has used real money. All three preregistered failures asked for hypothetical donations, and Maier and colleagues say so themselves, calling for high-powered replications with real money run as registered reports and in collaboration with proponents of the effect. The real-money evidence is small and old: Small, Loewenstein and Slovic's four studies ran on 121, 99, 159 and 165 people, and Kogut and Ritov's on 153 and 185 Hebrew University students. Lee and Feeley's meta-analysis could not be read on this pass, so nothing is quoted from it here beyond what Maier's reanalysis attests. It is not paywalled. Unpaywall, OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar all record it free at the publisher, but Taylor and Francis answered four different user agents with a Cloudflare challenge on 21 September 2026, and the Wayback Machine excludes that host on robots grounds. No repository copy is listed by Crossref, OpenAlex, CORE or the authors' institutional portal. Its moderator analyses, its heterogeneity statistics and the share of its 41 effects that measured real money are therefore left off this page rather than guessed at. A corrigendum to it exists, published on 3 July 2017, and is closed by the same challenge. The effect also does not travel across recipients. Deshpande and Spears ran three randomised experiments in India, one of them 56,000 purchased online advertisements, and report an identifiable victim effect for generic Indian, high-caste and Muslim recipients that is "absent or reversed for low-caste recipients". Searches on 21 September 2026 of OpenAlex, Crossref, the OSF preprint index and the published record found no multi-laboratory replication project covering the effect, and none from the Psychological Science Accelerator or the Many Labs series. Bhati and Hansen, reviewing 187 experimental fundraising papers published between 2007 and 2019, add a separate objection: studies of the identified victim often stereotype the beneficiary in order to produce guilt in the donor.
misreadings: The famous pair of numbers is one study, not the paper. The $2.38 against $1.14 comes from Study 3 of Small, Loewenstein and Slovic, and that paper's other three studies are less obliging. Study 2, on 99 people, found no main effect of identifiability at all, F(1, 95) = .073, p = .79. Study 4, on 165 people, likewise found none, F(1, 160) = .87, p = .35. The paper is a study of what deliberation does to giving, not a demonstration that faces beat numbers. Two of its studies also print a main effect and a simple effect as the same F statistic. In Study 2 the pair carries the same p value as well; in Study 4, F(1, 160) = 3.49 appears as a main effect at p = .063 and as a simple effect at p < .01, with different effect sizes attached, which the entry could not reconcile. The second misreading is about what the effect is a contrast with. Kogut and Ritov's real-money experiment found the gap between one victim and eight only when both were identified; pooled across the identification conditions, the single victim's advantage did not reach significance, p = .144. Their next experiment showed the advantage vanishing when the two appeals were put side by side, with the group drawing 3.05 shekels against the single victim's 2.45, p = .46. So the effect is a separate-evaluation phenomenon about one identified person, which is not the mass-versus-individual story it is usually told as. Third, the photograph. Fundraising advice treats a face as the active ingredient. Jenni and Loewenstein found the opposite in the paper that named the effect, with the photographed victim drawing the least concern. Finally, the Baby Jessica anecdote. Jenni and Loewenstein date the rescue to late 1987; Small, Loewenstein and Slovic date it to 1987 in their introduction, while the stimulus text they gave their participants says 1989.

sources.text: Jenni, K. E., & Loewenstein, G. F. (1997). Explaining the "identifiable victim effect". Journal of Risk and Uncertainty, 14(3), 235-257. Read in full from Loewenstein's own page at Carnegie Mellon, which serves the published article that Springer sells. The figure of 127 respondents for Study 1 appears nowhere in it and has been replaced by the three counts the paper prints.

Small, D. A., Loewenstein, G., & Slovic, P. (2007). Sympathy and callousness: The impact of deliberative thought on donations to identifiable and statistical victims. Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, 102(2), 143-153. Read in full from Loewenstein's page at Carnegie Mellon. The Study 3 means are printed only as labels on Figure 3.

Kogut, T., & Ritov, I. (2005). The "identified victim" effect: An identified group, or just a single individual? Journal of Behavioral Decision Making, 18(3), 157-167. Read in full from the second author's page at the Hebrew University. Its Study 2 analysed 112 undergraduates, not the 120 named in Majumder's power-analysis paragraph.

Kogut, T., & Ritov, I. (2005). The singularity effect of identified victims in separate and joint evaluations. Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes, 97(2), 106-116. Read in full from the second author's page at the Hebrew University, which serves the published article that Elsevier sells. An earlier pass called this paper paywalled and reported nothing from it, which was wrong.

Lee, S., & Feeley, T. H. (2016). The identifiable victim effect: A meta-analytic review. Social Influence, 11(3), 199-215. Not obtained. Listed free at the publisher by Unpaywall, OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar, but Taylor and Francis answered four user agents with a Cloudflare challenge on 21 September 2026, the Wayback Machine excludes that host, and no repository copy is listed. Only what Maier's reanalysis attests about it is reported here. A corrigendum, DOI 10.1080/15534510.2017.1340136, is closed by the same challenge.

Maier, M., Wong, Y. C., & Feldman, G. (2024). Revisiting and rethinking the identifiable victim effect: Replication and extension of Small, Loewenstein, and Slovic (2007). Collabra: Psychology, 9(1), 90203. Read in full from the corresponding author's copy at mgto.org; the publisher's own site answered with a Cloudflare challenge. The authors call it a far replication with hypothetical donations, not a close one. The article carries a 2024 citation line inside a 2023 volume.

Majumder, R., Tai, Y. L., Ziano, I., & Feldman, G. (2024). Revisiting the impact of singularity on the identified victim effect: Replication and extension of Kogut and Ritov (2005a) Study 2. Judgment and Decision Making, 19, e26. Read in full from Cambridge Core. Majumder's initial is R., for Rajarshi, and Tai's is Y. L.

Mayiwar, L., Yu, S., Jeong, Y., Do, T., Rudko, I., Rekdal, R., Dorotic, M., & Feldman, G. (2026). Revisiting singularity and compassion fade: Replication and extensions of Experiments 1a and 3 in Västfjäll et al. (2014). PsyArXiv preprint, posted 20 August 2026. A preprint, not a published article. Read in full from the current posted version, whose extension adds the statistical condition used here. Its target is compassion fade, entry 232.

Lesner, T. H., & Rasmussen, O. D. (2014). The identifiable victim effect in charitable giving: Evidence from a natural field experiment. Applied Economics, 46(36), 4409-4430. Not obtained. Taylor and Francis answered with a Cloudflare challenge on 21 September 2026 and no repository copy holds a file. The sentence quoted here and the figure of 25,797 come from the publisher's abstract as carried by the University of Southern Denmark research portal, and nothing else from this paper is used.

Moche, H., Karlsson, H., & Västfjäll, D. (2024). Victim identifiability, number of victims, and unit asking in charitable giving. PLOS ONE, 19(3), e0300863. Read in full from the publisher. Identifiability moved affective ratings in Study 4 even where it did not move donations.

Deshpande, A., & Spears, D. (2016). Who is the identifiable victim? Caste and charitable giving in modern India. Economic Development and Cultural Change, 64(2), 299-321. Read in full from the version of record hosted by the r.i.c.e. institute. An earlier pass quoted this paper as saying "absent or even reversed"; it says "absent or reversed", and it reports the effect holding for Muslim recipients too. The 2012 working paper under a different title is one survey experiment, not three, and is not this article.

Bhati, A., & Hansen, R. K. (2020). A literature review of experimental studies in fundraising. Journal of Behavioral Public Administration, 3(1), 1-19. Read in full from the publisher. The sentence about stereotyping the beneficiary to foster guilt is the authors' own, in their abstract.
